title: Origin of mammals
summary: Analysis of the jaws of Brasilodon quadrangularis, a mouse-sized animal from southern Brazil dated to about 225 million years ago, found mammal-style tooth replacement. The authors say this pushes the origin of that trait, and possibly of mammals, back about 20 million years. Morganucodon and other Late Triassic to Jurassic animals are usually counted as the first mammal-like forms.

uncertainty.note: Start reflects the 225.42 ± 0.37 Ma radiometric date of the upper Candelária Sequence yielding Brasilodon; end marks the Triassic-Jurassic boundary by which mammaliaforms like Morganucodon were established.

where.modern_name: Linha São Luiz, Faxinal do Soturno, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil (type locality of Brasilodon quadrangularis; transition from cynodonts to mammaliaforms occurred across Pangaea)
where.historical_name: Southern Paraná Basin in southwestern Pangaea, Late Triassic; no polities existed

importance.justification: The origin of mammals established endothermy, diphyodont dentition, lactation, and high metabolic performance in vertebrates, producing the clade that became ecologically dominant across Cenozoic terrestrial and marine realms.

related.because: The initial origin of amniotes produced the synapsid lineage from which cynodonts and mammaliaforms evolved.
The Mesozoic origin of mammals provided the lineages that underwent adaptive radiation following the Chicxulub impact.
Mammalian diversification established the placental crown orders, including primates.
Ecosystem recovery after the Permian-Triassic extinction fostered cynodont therapsid diversification toward mammals.
